question: An Albert stain of a throat swab shows yellow-green bacilli with blue-black polar granules arranged in a Chinese letter pattern. Which test should be performed next to confirm that this isolate produces diphtheria toxin?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Elek's test is an immunodiffusion assay where the isolate is streaked perpendicular to an antitoxin-impregnated filter paper strip. A precipitation arc confirms toxin production — only toxigenic strains (carrying phage β with the tox gene) cause clinical disease.
The PYR (pyrrolidonyl arylamidase) test identifies Group A Streptococcus and Enterococcus. It has no role in Corynebacterium identification or toxigenicity testing.
Optochin sensitivity distinguishes Streptococcus pneumoniae (sensitive, zone ≥14 mm) from other α-haemolytic streptococci. It is irrelevant for diphtheria diagnosis.
The Widal test detects agglutinating antibodies against Salmonella typhi O and H antigens and is used in the diagnosis of enteric (typhoid) fever, not diphtheria.

overallFeedback.feedback: Albert stain identifies C. diphtheriae morphologically. The next step is Elek's gel precipitation test — an in-vitro immunodiffusion assay that specifically detects diphtheria exotoxin production by the isolate.

Elek's test confirms toxigenicity — this distinction matters because non-toxigenic C. diphtheriae strains do not cause the membrane, myocarditis or neuropathy. Always administer diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) empirically in suspected cases while awaiting results.
